WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Congress passed a $300 billion farm bill over President Bush's veto for a second time Wednesday, a step made necessary by a clerical error when the original bill passed. Congress overrode President Bush's second veto of a $300 billion farm bill. The Senate voted 80-14 to approve the measure over Bush's objections, following a 317-109 vote in the House of Representatives. Both votes were well above the two-thirds majority needed to override the veto, which Bush delivered Wednesday morning. Congress overrode an earlier veto of the farm bill last month, even though lawmakers had discovered that 34 pages were missing in the version originally sent to the White House. In spiking the latest version, Bush said he objected to its continued subsidies for the wealthy and its use of budget gimmicks to hide a $20 billion increase in spending. But Sen. "This bill does not add to the deficit or debt, because this bill is paid for," he said. "That is not my claim. That is the finding of the Congressional Budget Office." The discovery of the missing section, Title III, prompted concerns from House Republicans that the override vote was improper. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said the sections of the bill that were originally sent to the president had become law after Congress voted to override Bush's first veto. But to put Title III into effect, Congress re-passed the entire legislation, including the missing pages, and resent it to Bush. The House voted 306-110 at the end of May. The Senate voted 77-15 for the bill at the beginning of June. Two-thirds of the $300 billion in spending for the farm bill will go for nutrition programs such as food stamps. Another $40 billion will go toward farm subsidies, and $30 billion is allocated for payments to farms to keep land idle and other environmental programs. After vetoing the latest version of the farm bill, Bush scolded Congress on Wednesday for not "modifying certain objectionable, onerous and fiscally imprudent provisions. ... I am returning this bill for the same reasons as stated in my veto message." When he vetoed the first version of the farm bill, Bush said it "continues subsidies for the wealthy and increases farm bill spending by more than $20 billion, while using budget gimmicks to hide much of the increase." The president said it would hurt efforts to improve American farmers' access to overseas markets. Congress has passed one other bill over Bush's objections: legislation for a $23 billion water project that the president vetoed in 2007. CNN Capitol Hill producer Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Congress overrode President Bush's veto of the $300 billion farm bill for a second time on Wednesday, a step rendered necessary by a clerical error that had marred the bill's original passage.

The Senate voted 80-14 to approve the measure over the president's objections, following a 317-109 vote in the House of Representatives. Both tallies exceeded by a comfortable margin the two-thirds majority required to override a veto—one that Bush had issued earlier that same morning.

Congress had already overridden an initial veto of the farm bill the previous month, only to discover afterward that 34 pages, constituting Title III, had been inadvertently omitted from the version originally transmitted to the White House.

In rejecting this latest iteration of the bill, Bush cited his continued opposition to subsidies benefiting wealthy recipients and criticized the legislation's reliance on budget gimmicks to obscure a $20 billion spending increase. Senator Kent Conrad, chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, disputed this characterization, asserting that the measure would actually reduce government expenditures by $110 million. "This bill does not add to the deficit or debt, because this bill is paid for," Conrad stated. "That is not my claim—that is the finding of the Congressional Budget Office."

The discovery of the missing Title III section had raised concerns among House Republicans regarding the propriety of the earlier override vote. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi maintained that the portions of the bill originally submitted to the president had already become law once Congress overrode Bush's first veto. Nevertheless, to formally enact Title III, Congress opted to re-pass the legislation in its entirety, missing pages included, and resubmitted it to the president. The House approved this complete version 306-110 in late May, followed by Senate passage of 77-15 in early June.

Of the bill's $300 billion in total spending, roughly two-thirds is designated for nutrition assistance programs such as food stamps. An additional $40 billion is earmarked for farm subsidies, while $30 billion will fund payments to farmers for leaving land fallow, along with other environmental initiatives.

Following his veto of this latest version, Bush admonished Congress on Wednesday for failing to address "certain objectionable, onerous and fiscally imprudent provisions," adding, "I am returning this bill for the same reasons as stated in my veto message." In his original veto statement, Bush had argued that the bill "continues subsidies for the wealthy and increases farm bill spending by more than $20 billion, while using budget gimmicks to hide much of the increase." He further contended that the legislation would undermine efforts to expand American farmers' access to international markets.

This marks only the second instance in which Congress has overridden a Bush veto—the first being a $23 billion water resources bill the president rejected in 2007.

Both tallies far surpassed the two-thirds majority threshold required by the Constitution to overturn a presidential veto, underscoring the broad, cross-party support the legislation commanded on Capitol Hill.

# Congress Overrides Second Veto of Farm Bill After Clerical Error Correction

In an unusual sequence of legislative events, Congress this week completed action on the $300 billion farm bill for a second time, addressing a rare procedural mishap that had inadvertently created confusion over the scope of the legislation President Bush had originally vetoed.

## The Clerical Error

When Congress first passed the massive farm bill and sent it to the White House, a clerical error resulted in 34 pages of the legislation being omitted from the version that was formally transmitted. This oversight meant that the bill President Bush vetoed did not actually represent the complete text that lawmakers had approved. Once the mistake was discovered, congressional leaders determined that the appropriate remedy was to re-pass the entire bill in its complete form, ensuring that the version sent to the president accurately reflected what both chambers had agreed upon.

## Second Veto

Rather than allowing the corrected legislation to become law, President Bush vetoed the complete bill a second time. In explaining his decision, the president reiterated concerns he had raised previously, chief among them being that the bill continued to provide subsidies to wealthy farmers who, in his view, did not need government assistance. Bush also criticized what he characterized as hidden spending increases buried within the legislation, arguing that the bill's true fiscal impact was being obscured from the public and from Congress.

## Congressional Response

Despite the president's objections, both chambers of Congress moved swiftly to override the veto, demonstrating that the broad bipartisan coalition supporting the farm bill remained firmly intact. The House of Representatives voted 317-109 to override, while the Senate followed with an even more lopsided margin of 80-14. These substantial majorities—well above the two-thirds threshold required in each chamber—underscored the depth of support for the legislation across party lines and reflected the political difficulty of opposing a bill with such wide-reaching implications for farmers, food assistance recipients, and rural communities.

## What the Bill Funds

The farm bill directs federal spending across several major categories. The largest share of funding is allocated to nutrition programs, which include food assistance initiatives that benefit millions of low-income Americans. The legislation also provides substantial subsidies to farmers, supporting agricultural production and helping stabilize commodity markets. Additionally, the bill includes funding for environmental initiatives aimed at conservation and sustainable land use practices tied to agricultural operations.

## Fiscal Impact

Notably, the Congressional Budget Office weighed in on the legislation's fiscal implications, concluding that rather than adding to the national debt, the bill would actually reduce the deficit by $110 million. This finding stood in contrast to the president's concerns about hidden spending increases, and it provided ammunition for supporters of the bill who argued that the legislation was both fiscally responsible and necessary to support American agriculture and food security programs.

## Outcome

With both chambers successfully overriding the veto by comfortable margins, the farm bill became law despite the president's objections. The episode marked a significant moment in the relationship between the executive and legislative branches, highlighting Congress's willingness to assert its will on a matter of broad bipartisan consensus, even in the face of repeated presidential opposition. The successful override also brought closure to what had become an unusually complicated legislative process, one marked by an administrative error that added an extra layer of procedural drama to an already contentious policy debate.

**Congress Overrides Bush's Second Veto of Farm Bill After Clerical Error Forces Do-Over**

*WASHINGTON (CNN)* — The Senate voted Thursday to override President Bush's veto of the massive farm bill for the second time in as many weeks, capping off an extraordinary legislative saga that saw lawmakers forced to pass the same bill twice after a clerical error left an entire section out of the version originally sent to the White House.

The Senate voted 80-14 to override the veto, following a similar 317-109 vote in the House on Wednesday. The overrides mean the $290 billion farm bill will become law over the president's objections, despite his insistence that the legislation is too costly and provides unnecessary subsidies to wealthy farmers.

"This is a good bill for America's farmers, for America's families, and for our country," said Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman Tom Harkin, D-Iowa. "The president was wrong to veto it the first time, and he was wrong to veto it the second time."

The unusual second veto stemmed from an embarrassing mistake by Congress. When lawmakers sent the original bill to Bush last month, a clerical error resulted in a 34-page section on international food aid and trade programs being omitted entirely from the document that reached the president's desk. Bush vetoed that incomplete version on May 21, and while both chambers voted to override, questions quickly arose about whether the override was even valid, given that the bill Congress had passed differed from the one actually sent to the White House.

To resolve the confusion, congressional leaders opted to start over, passing the complete and correct version of the bill last week. Bush vetoed it again Wednesday, setting up Thursday's rare second override.

"We wanted to make sure there was no question, no ambiguity, about the validity of this legislation," said House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif. "Farmers and families across this country are counting on the certainty this bill provides, and we were not going to let a technical error stand in the way."

White House press secretary Dana Perino said the mix-up did not change the administration's fundamental objections to the bill's cost and structure.

"Whether it's the right bill or the wrong bill, it's still the wrong policy," Perino said. "This legislation continues subsidies to farmers who don't need them, at a time when commodity prices are at record highs and family budgets are being squeezed by rising food costs."

The farm bill, which authorizes programs ranging from crop subsidies to food stamps to conservation initiatives, is typically renewed every five years and has historically drawn bipartisan support due to its wide-ranging benefits for both rural and urban lawmakers' constituents.

Critics of the bill, including some fiscal conservatives and reform advocates, argue that the legislation continues to funnel taxpayer money to large agribusinesses rather than the small family farms it purports to support. Supporters counter that the bill also expands funding for nutrition assistance, land conservation, and renewable energy programs.

Despite the embarrassing procedural stumble, congressional leaders sought to project confidence that the twin overrides sent a clear message.

"Mistakes happen — this was a paperwork issue, nothing more," said Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev. "What matters is that this bill is now, unquestionably, the law of the land."

The episode marks only the second time in Bush's presidency that Congress has successfully overridden one of his vetoes, and is believed to be the first instance in modern history in which lawmakers were forced to override the same bill twice due to an administrative mishap.

With the override now complete, the Agriculture Department is expected to begin implementing the bill's provisions in the coming weeks.

# Congress Passes $290 Billion Farm Bill Over Presidential Veto; Nutrition Programs Claim Lion's Share of Funding

**WASHINGTON** — After months of negotiation and a rare veto override, the 2008 Farm Bill — formally titled the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act — became law this week, authorizing roughly $290 billion in spending over five years. The legislation touched nearly every corner of American agriculture and food policy, from crop subsidies to nutrition assistance to conservation incentives, and became a flashpoint between the Bush administration and congressional leaders in both parties.

## Spending Breakdown

According to Congressional Budget Office estimates, the bill's spending was distributed roughly as follows:

- **Nutrition Programs (~67% of total spending, over $200 billion):** The largest single component of the bill funds the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP, then still commonly called food stamps), along with emergency food assistance and nutrition education programs. Lawmakers expanded eligibility and increased benefit levels, citing rising food costs and economic strain on low-income families.

- **Commodity Subsidies (approximately $35–40 billion):** Direct payments, counter-cyclical payments, and price supports for corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton, and rice growers made up the traditional core of farm bill spending. The legislation retained the direct-payment structure that critics said continued to benefit large and wealthy agribusiness operations regardless of market prices.

- **Conservation and Environmental Programs (approximately $25–28 billion):** Funding was directed toward land conservation, wetlands protection, and working-lands stewardship programs such as the Conservation Reserve Program and the Environmental Quality Incentives Program, aimed at reducing runoff, preserving habitat, and supporting sustainable farming practices.

- **Crop Insurance and Disaster Assistance (approximately $22 billion):** The bill created a permanent agricultural disaster relief fund and expanded federal crop insurance subsidies, a provision farm-state lawmakers said was necessary given increasingly volatile weather patterns.

- **Rural Development, Energy, and Other Titles (remaining balance):** Smaller allocations supported rural infrastructure, biofuel research and production incentives, and specialty crop and organic farming initiatives.

## Political Reactions

**President Bush**, who vetoed the bill twice, argued it was too costly and failed to sufficiently reform subsidy payments to high-income farmers. In his veto messages, Bush contended that at a time of record farm income, the bill should have tightened eligibility caps for subsidy recipients rather than expanding overall spending. He characterized the legislation as fiscally irresponsible and said it sent the wrong signal to taxpayers during a period of economic uncertainty.

**Speaker Nancy Pelosi** championed the bill as a victory for working families, family farmers, and conservation efforts. She argued the legislation struck a necessary balance — supporting struggling farmers while dramatically boosting nutrition assistance for Americans facing rising grocery costs. Pelosi criticized the president's veto as out of touch with the needs of both rural and urban constituencies, and she pressed for the swift veto-override votes that ultimately succeeded in both chambers with substantial bipartisan majorities.

**Senator Kent Conrad** of North Dakota, chairman of the Senate Budget Committee and a key negotiator on the bill, defended its fiscal design, noting that the legislation was largely paid for through offsets and closed tax loopholes rather than new deficit spending. Conrad emphasized the bill's disaster-assistance provisions and conservation title as critical for farmers in his home state and across the Great Plains, and he pushed back on the administration's characterization of the bill as unreformed, pointing to payment limitation changes included in the final text.

## Outcome

Despite the president's objections, both the House and Senate voted by wide, veto-proof margins to override Bush's rejection, allowing the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act to take effect. The override marked one of the more significant legislative defeats of the Bush administration's second term and set federal agriculture and nutrition policy through the following five years.

# Congress Overrides Farm Bill Veto in Rare Bipartisan Rebuke

WASHINGTON — In a striking display of bipartisan defiance, both chambers of Congress voted to override a presidential veto of the massive farm bill this week, marking one of the few times in recent history that lawmakers have united across party lines to overcome a White House objection.

The $290 billion farm bill, which includes subsidies for farmers, funding for nutrition assistance programs, and conservation initiatives, had been vetoed by the President, who argued the legislation was too costly and included wasteful spending provisions that favored special interests over taxpayers.

Despite the administration's objections, the override votes passed with significant margins in both the House and Senate, reflecting the deep support the farm bill enjoys among lawmakers from agricultural states — and the political risks of opposing legislation that touches everything from crop insurance to food stamps.

"This bill provides certainty for our farmers and ranchers who feed this nation," said one senior lawmaker following the vote. "It's disappointing the President chose to veto it, but Congress has spoken clearly."

## A Familiar Pattern

The override marks the second time in recent years that Congress has banded together to overturn a presidential veto on major spending legislation. In 2007, lawmakers similarly overrode a veto of the Water Resources Development Act, a sprawling public works bill authorizing billions of dollars for flood control, dredging, and other water infrastructure projects across the country.

That override, like this week's action on the farm bill, underscored the political potency of legislation that delivers tangible benefits to lawmakers' home districts and states. The 2007 water projects bill had drawn presidential criticism for its price tag and the inclusion of hundreds of local projects — often derided by critics as pork-barrel spending — but it sailed through both chambers with veto-proof majorities, as members from both parties were reluctant to be seen blocking funding for projects benefiting their constituents.

The parallel between the two overrides highlights a recurring dynamic in Washington: while presidents of both parties have often railed against the cost and contents of these sprawling bills, individual lawmakers face strong incentives to support legislation that funnels federal dollars into their districts, whether for water projects, farm subsidies, or nutrition programs.

## Political Dynamics at Play

Veto overrides remain relatively rare in American politics, requiring a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate — a high bar that reflects the framers' intent to make presidential vetoes difficult to overcome except in cases of strong bipartisan consensus.

The farm bill's broad coalition of support — spanning rural agricultural interests, urban legislators concerned with nutrition assistance, and environmental advocates focused on conservation provisions — proved sufficient to reach that threshold, much as the water resources bill had drawn support from lawmakers concerned with flood protection, port infrastructure, and economic development in their regions.

Critics of both bills have pointed to their sheer size and scope as evidence of Congress's difficulty in reining in spending, even when a sitting president explicitly calls for restraint. Supporters counter that both pieces of legislation address critical infrastructure and economic needs that individual, piecemeal bills would struggle to accomplish.

## Looking Ahead

With the farm bill now law despite the President's objections, attention turns to implementation of its various programs, including new conservation initiatives and adjustments to commodity support programs. The override also serves as a reminder of the limits of presidential power when facing determined, bipartisan majorities in Congress — and may offer a preview of future clashes over spending priorities as the administration continues to push for fiscal restraint against a Congress often more attuned to local and regional interests.

The episode adds to a small but notable list of successful veto overrides in modern American history, joining the 2007 water resources bill as examples of Congress's willingness to assert its constitutional authority when consensus proves strong enough to overcome presidential objections.
